# Extended worked examples

[Back to the main reference](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430%20-%20Accounting%20and%20Finance)

The main note contains the short methods and connected bookkeeping example. This note preserves longer reconciliations and source comparisons. Amounts are £ unless indicated. These worked solutions are independently calculated study material; they are not presented as official marking schemes.

## Royal Limited source check

The supplied solution image shows cash on hand £4,000, bank £5,500, inventory £3,000, receivables £1,000 and van £3,000. Assets total **£16,500**; payables £6,500 and equity £10,000 balance to the same total. “Van on Credit” is displayed as zero.

The associated Exercise 1.2 says £1,000 rent covers the first quarter, while the image has no prepaid-rent asset. Its displayed amounts are consistent with expensing that £1,000 in full. If the reporting period is January alone, the rent is consumed evenly over the three months and no other changes are introduced, the later accrual method implies:

| Item | Displayed solution | Conditional January accrual treatment |
|---|---:|---:|
| Rent expense | Consistent with £1,000 charged | £333.33 |
| Prepaid rent asset | Not shown | £666.67 |
| Total assets | £16,500 | £17,166.67 |
| Liabilities | £6,500 | £6,500 |
| Equity | £10,000 | £10,666.67 |

The conditional adjustment is not a transcription of the official image. It follows from a different explicit period-end assumption. The task and solution also have inconsistent year labels. A balanced total does not settle those issues. No extra depreciation has been assumed in the adjusted comparison.

Sources: [Exercise 1.2](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/126878.pdf%23page%3D1) and [the original solution image](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/128133.png).

## Chapter 2 daily trading statements

The modified home assignment starts with an £800 owner investment. Assume all purchases and sales are cash, inventory cost is proportional to the fraction sold, and there are no other expenses or owner movements.

| Day | Inventory bought | Sales | Cost of sales | Daily profit | Closing cash | Closing inventory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Monday | 600 | 200 | 150 | 50 | 400 | 450 |
| Tuesday | 300 | 900 | 750 | 150 | 1,000 | 0 |
| Wednesday | 500 | 400 | 375 | 25 | 900 | 125 |
| Thursday | 0 | 100 | 125 | −25 | 1,000 | 0 |

Monday's £150 cost is one-quarter of £600, not the £600 cash purchase. Tuesday's cost is the opening £450 inventory plus £300 purchased. Wednesday sells three-quarters of £500, leaving £125 for Thursday. Total profit is £200; final cash £1,000 equals initial capital £800 plus £200 profit.

At each date, assets are cash + remaining inventory. With no liabilities, equity equals those assets. The equity sequence £850, £1,000, £1,025, £1,000 changes by each day's profit. The first day's cash-flow statement includes the £800 owner contribution as financing; the income statement does not call it revenue.

Source: [Chapter 2 home assignment](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/132531.pdf%23page%3D1). The introductory lecture example has different starting figures; do not mix them.

## Chapter 5 home assignment

**Scale: £ million.** The source provides 2022/2023 statements, 2023 profit before tax £38m, depreciation £24m, interest expense/paid £5m and dividends £20m. It states no asset disposals. Use unchanged borrowing/share-capital figures and no other non-cash capital additions. The source PDF carries an old printed deadline; the current assignment's date is determined by Canvas, not that printed heading.

### Operating reconciliation

| Step | Effect (£m) | Explanation |
|---|---:|---|
| Profit before tax after interest | 38 | Starting profit supplied |
| Add depreciation | +24 | Non-cash expense |
| Add interest expense | +5 | Actual interest paid deducted later |
| Inventory falls 28 → 27 | +1 | Releases working capital |
| Receivables fall 30 → 28 | +2 | Releases working capital |
| Payables fall 42 → 34 | −8 | Supplier payments exceed the corresponding accrual increase |
| **Cash generated** | **62** | Before cash interest, tax and dividends |
| Interest paid | −5 | Expense equals payment in the facts |
| Tax paid: 9 opening + 9 expense − 5 closing | −13 | Tax liability reconciliation |
| Dividends paid | −20 | Course slide-13 classification |
| **Net operating cash** | **24** | Course presentation |

### Investing and the cash check

Closing equipment/property carrying amount £210m = opening £185m + additions − £24m depreciation. With no disposals, revaluations or non-cash additions, additions and cash capex are **£49m**. Borrowings and share capital are unchanged, so there is no other financing cash flow under these facts.

$$
\Delta Cash=24-49+0=-25\text{ million}.
$$

Opening cash £22m minus £25m gives closing **−£3m**, matching the overdraft. If dividends are shown as financing instead, operating becomes £44m and financing becomes −£20m. The total remains −£25m. Never deduct dividends in both categories.

Sources: [home-assignment statements](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/166033.pdf%23page%3D1) and [course classification template](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/158749.pdf%23page%3D13). The locked home-assignment solution was unavailable; this is an independently checked reconstruction, not a recovered official answer.

### Another supplied cash bridge

The Chapter 5 examples PDF starts from profit before tax after interest 122, depreciation 34, interest expense 6; inventory rises 15 → 17, receivables fall 24 → 21 and payables rise 18 → 19. Cash generated is:

$$122+34+6-2+3+1=164.$$

Subtract interest paid 5, tax paid 32 and dividends paid 9 in the supplied layout to obtain **118 net operating cash**. This preserves the source's scale; it is a different dataset from the £m home-assignment statements above. Source: [Chapter 5 examples](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/158750.pdf%23page%3D1).

## Course capstone

Source: [Chapter 10, physical PDF pages 49–55](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/178645.pdf%23page%3D49). This is the verified extended reconciliation retained from the earlier reference, with narrower tables to improve reading.

### 1. Establish the independent timelines

Pay £50,000 for a machine at $t=0$. It lasts five years, has zero disposal value and is depreciated straight line at £10,000/year. Produce 3,000 units annually. Manufacturing cash cost is £6,000 in years 1–2 and £7,500 in years 3–5. Sell at £8/unit. No tax, interest or storage cost is specified. Finished goods use the exercise's LIFO convention for internal valuation.

| Year | Units sold | Current-year cash-sale units | Earlier collection | Receipts |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 3,000 | 2,000 | 0 | 16,000 |
| 2 | 2,000 | 2,000 | 0 | 16,000 |
| 3 | 2,500 | 2,000 | 8,000 from year 1 | 24,000 |
| 4 | 3,000 | 3,000 | 0 | 24,000 |
| 5 | 4,500 | 4,500 | 4,000 from year 3 | 40,000 |

Revenue follows the units sold. Receipts follow the payment terms. At year 2, the £8,000 receivable from year 1 still exists; it is collected in year 3. A new £4,000 receivable then remains until year 5.

### 2. Price inventory layers and cost of sales

Years 1–2 production costs £2/unit; years 3–5 costs £2.50/unit. With LIFO, each sale first consumes the newest available layer.

| Year | Production cost paid | Cost of goods sold | Closing inventory | Closing receivables |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 6,000 | 6,000 | 0 | 8,000 |
| 2 | 6,000 | 4,000 | 2,000 | 8,000 |
| 3 | 7,500 | 6,250 | 3,250 | 4,000 |
| 4 | 7,500 | 7,500 | 3,250 | 4,000 |
| 5 | 7,500 | 10,750 | 0 | 0 |

Year 3 sells 2,500 of that year's 3,000 units at £2.50. Its closing inventory is the older 1,000 × £2 plus the remaining 500 × £2.50 = £3,250. Year 4 sells its current production, leaving those older layers unchanged. Year 5 sells all remaining units, so its cost is £7,500 current production + £3,250 opening inventory = £10,750.

### 3. Calculate cash flow and accounting profit separately

| Date / year | Cash flow | Revenue | Depreciation | Net income |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | −50,000 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 10,000 | 24,000 | 10,000 | 8,000 |
| 2 | 10,000 | 16,000 | 10,000 | 2,000 |
| 3 | 16,500 | 20,000 | 10,000 | 3,750 |
| 4 | 16,500 | 24,000 | 10,000 | 6,500 |
| 5 | 32,500 | 36,000 | 10,000 | 15,250 |

For $t\ge1$, cash flow is receipts minus production cash outflow; net income is revenue minus cost of goods sold minus depreciation. The initial machine purchase is a cash outflow, not a £50,000 expense in year 0.

At $r=10\%$:

$$
NPV=-50{,}000+\frac{10{,}000}{1.1}+\frac{10{,}000}{1.1^2}
+\frac{16{,}500}{1.1^3}+\frac{16{,}500}{1.1^4}+\frac{32{,}500}{1.1^5}
=\boxed{£11{,}201.73}.
$$

Discounting the accounting-profit column gives **£25,651.69**. That is not project NPV. Different recognition dates matter even though total profit and total net cash both equal £35,500 after the investment and terminal clearing.

### 4. Charge for the capital still tied up

Operating assets are machine carrying amount + inventory + receivables in this exercise. There are no operating payables in the supplied simplified facts. Use the **opening**, not closing, balance for each year's capital charge.

| Year | Opening operating assets | Net income | 10% capital charge | Residual income |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 50,000 | 8,000 | 5,000 | 3,000 |
| 2 | 48,000 | 2,000 | 4,800 | −2,800 |
| 3 | 40,000 | 3,750 | 4,000 | −250 |
| 4 | 27,250 | 6,500 | 2,725 | 3,775 |
| 5 | 17,250 | 15,250 | 1,725 | 13,525 |

Year 1 closes with operating assets £40,000 machine + £8,000 receivables = £48,000. Year 2 closes at £30,000 + £2,000 + £8,000 = £40,000. Years 3–4 close at £27,250 and £17,250. Year 5 clears all balances to zero.

$$
PV(RI)=\frac{3{,}000}{1.1}-\frac{2{,}800}{1.1^2}-\frac{250}{1.1^3}
+\frac{3{,}775}{1.1^4}+\frac{13{,}525}{1.1^5}
=\boxed{£11{,}201.73}=NPV.
$$

The independent calculation script rebuilds LIFO layers, receipts, capital balances and all five annual roll-forwards. It does not merely compare transcribed totals. Use NPV or the consistent full discounted RI series to assess value. A year's positive accounting profit alone does not establish adequate return on capital.

## Rounding in the radio example

The newly present tutoring-session 5 solution rounds minimum sales up to 12,728 radios. It therefore reports break-even sales £763,680 and a 7,272-radio/£436,320 safety margin. The main note also shows the theoretical fractional threshold 12,727.27 and its corresponding £763,636.36 sales and £436,363.64 safety margin. These are different explicit rounding conventions, not conflicting cost assumptions. Keep whole-unit decisions and continuous-model comparisons separate.

Sources: [the question](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/177122.pdf%23page%3D1) and [the tutoring solution](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/185220.pdf%23page%3D1).
